title: Substrate types and bonding
audience: Plasterers and plastering workers at the basic level, and handyman workers who patch plaster
learningOutcomes: Identify the common plaster substrates and their bonding behaviour.
Select a bonding agent or key coat suited to the substrate and the finish.
Identify moisture and movement that must be resolved before plaster is applied.

instruction.heading: Know the substrate
instruction.body: Plaster bonds differently to each substrate. Plasterboard has a paper face that takes a plaster finish when the joints are set correctly. Masonry is porous and may need a bonding agent or a scratch coat to key the plaster. Lime-based older plaster can be soft, crumbly or bonded poorly to its backing, and it needs assessment before a cement-based coat is applied over it. Render and concrete may carry salts, dust or release agent that stop bonding. Identify the substrate and its condition before choosing the coat.

instruction.heading: Bonding and moisture
instruction.body: Bonding fails when the substrate is dusty, greasy, damp or too smooth. Clean and dry the surface, and use a bonding agent or key coat that the product data sheet recommends for the substrate. Check for damp before plastering, because plaster laid on a moisture source will fail and hide the cause. Movement at junctions or cracks can cause the finish to crack later, so note movement and refer it before the coat is applied. A plaster that bonds well to a sound substrate and dries evenly is the result of checking these points first. Before you accept plaster work, check the licence threshold for its value. In New South Wales the figure is more than $5,000 of labour and materials, GST included, for dry and wet plastering (NSW Government pages, last updated 23 June 2026).

procedure: Identify the substrate type and its condition, and record it.
Check for damp, salts, dust, grease and movement.
Clean and dry the substrate as the product data sheet requires.
Select a bonding agent or key coat suited to the substrate and the finish.
Apply the bonding product and let it reach the state the data sheet requires before plastering.
Refer any damp, movement or older soft plaster before the coat is applied, and record the referral.

workedExamples.situation: A plaster patch is to be applied to an older lime plaster wall that feels soft, with a crack running from the corner of a window.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the cement patch be applied directly?
workedExamples.reasoning: Not directly. The soft lime plaster may not bond to a cement-based patch, and the crack suggests movement. Assess the substrate and the crack, refer the movement, and select a compatible repair method after the assessment. Record the referral.

equipmentAndPpe: Bonding agent or key coat per data sheet
Dust mask suited to the task

commonErrors.error: Applying a cement patch to soft lime plaster without assessment.
commonErrors.prevention: Assess the substrate and refer before choosing the repair method.
Find and record the moisture source before plastering.

commonErrors.error: Skipping the bonding agent on a smooth or sealed surface.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the bonding agent or key coat the data sheet recommends for the substrate.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: New South Wales: dry plastering (rigid sheeting, cornices and ceilings) needs a contractor licence above $5,000 of labour and materials, GST included (NSW Government page, last updated 23 June 2026). Wet plastering, also called solid plastering, has the same $5,000 threshold (NSW Government page, last updated 23 June 2026).

Queensland: plastering solid and plastering drywall are QBCC classes (both pages last reviewed 31 August 2021). The $3,300 figure on those pages is the limit for incidental work outside the class, not a building-work threshold.

Victoria: plastering-only jobs need no registration (Consumer Victoria page, last updated 9 July 2025). The page says “You must register with the BPC if you are using a combination of skills (such as plastering and painting) to complete a job.”
Completing this lesson does not give a plastering licence, certificate or authority to undertake regulated building work.

qualityStandard: The substrate type and condition are recorded before a coat is chosen.
No plaster is applied over damp or unresolved movement.
The bonding product is the one the data sheet recommends for the substrate.
documentationEvidence: Substrate record with type, condition and bonding product
Referral note for any damp, movement or soft plaster
summary: Identify the substrate, because each bonds differently.
Clean, dry and key the substrate as the data sheet requires.
Resolve or refer damp, movement and soft older plaster before plastering.

knowledgeChecks.question: A cement patch is to be applied to soft lime plaster with a crack. What is correct?
options: Apply the cement patch directly over the soft lime, since it will bond quickly and hold
Assess the substrate and the crack, and refer the movement before choosing a compatible method
Fill the crack and skim over it with the same cement mix used for the whole patch today
Paint the wall instead, since the crack will be hidden under the new paint coat easily

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must damp be found before plastering?
options: Damp makes plaster harder and more durable over the years
Damp has no effect on plaster at all, so no check is needed
Plaster laid on a moisture source will fail and can hide the cause
Damp only affects the paint on the surface of the wall and nothing else

knowledgeChecks.question: How does the lesson say to choose a bonding agent or key coat?
options: Pick the cheapest product on the shelf
Use whatever the last job used
Use the one the product data sheet recommends for the substrate
Choose by the colour of the wall
